This plan started as `yr-pre-ml-PLAN-v001.md`, written on 2026-11-23 in a Claude Code chat with the instructor
(Prof. Rosenthal). The same day, the instructor answered its open questions, and the repository was set up. That
file is now in `oldfiles/`, which git does not track. This document replaces it: change the plan here.

## How to use this plan {#sec-how}

- Read the whole plan before you start a step. @sec-decisions lists the decisions; all of them are made now.
- **Other repositories are read-only.** yrThinkPython, aiasdSrc, yrS4 and yrProject are other repositories. Read
  them; do not change them. Write only inside this repository, unless the instructor says otherwise.
- **Do not touch yrProject's repository** while its book-tools work is in progress (the instructor, 2026-11-23).
  `yrProject.sh update` runs here with `--no-register`. Reading its templates and running `yrProject.sh check`
  are fine.
- **No dependency on yrThinkPython** (the instructor, 2026-11-23). This book can copy and adapt a file from
  yrThinkPython. The copy is then this book's own file. Nothing in this repository runs a file from yrThinkPython,
  uses its virtual environments, or refers to its paths. @sec-copies lists the copies.
- Steps marked **(instructor runs)** are commands that the Claude Code classifier refuses, or that change live
  systems. Give the instructor the exact command, one at a time.
- Do not commit, push or publish unless the instructor asks. Add files to git by path, never `git add -A`. A push
  to `main` publishes the website.
- Older files that are kept, not deleted yet, go into `oldfiles/` (the instructor's convention). Git does not
  track that folder.

## Background {#sec-background}

- **Course:** an undergraduate business-school Python course. Students first learn basic Python from *Think
  Python* (the instructor's fork, a Jupyter Book with Colab links). The course then has **eight lectures of 75
  minutes** that prepare students for machine learning (ML). Almost all of that time teaches NumPy and pandas. ML
  itself appears only as motivation (the first part) and as prepared code in the two final integrated exercises.
- **Environment:** students use **Thonny** in class. The book is written **Colab-first**: each chapter is a
  notebook that opens in Google Colab. A short chapter explains how to run the same code in Thonny and other IDEs.
- **What the instructor wants:** an approachable, free, online text in the style of *Think Python* (short steps,
  small examples, gentle explanations). An earlier ChatGPT discussion looked for an existing book (McKinney,
  VanderPlas, Downey's *Elements of Data Science*, OpenStax). None of them fits well, so the instructor writes this
  one. Those books become "further reading" links only.
- **The infrastructure:** the book is a **yrProject** (rules, skills, GitHub issues, project docs) and a
  **subjexts (yrS4) package** (labels in the margin, a table of contents by label, author notes and in-place
  edits, the AI tutor).

### Lessons from the ChatGPT discussion (keep them in the book) {#sec-lessons}

1. **The display difference.** In Colab, a bare expression such as `df.head()` on the last line of a cell shows
   its value. In a Thonny script it shows nothing: students must write `print(df.head())`, or type the
   expression in Thonny's Shell. The book uses Colab style, so the "Colab, Thonny and other IDEs" chapter
   explains this first, and the first chapters repeat it in a reminder box.
2. **Real business data breaks scikit-learn.** Missing values (`NaN`) and text columns make `fit()` fail. So the
   book teaches `isna()`, `dropna()`, `fillna()` and `pd.get_dummies()` before the two projects.
3. **Keep the ML demo inside scikit-learn.** No XGBoost. Use `LinearRegression`, `DecisionTreeRegressor` and
   `RandomForestRegressor`. Colab has scikit-learn already; Thonny users install one package fewer.
4. **Connect NumPy to ML.** The part "Working with arrays" ends with `X` (a 2-D array of predictors), `y` (a 1-D
   array, the target), their `.shape`, and `df.to_numpy()`. This is the reason NumPy matters for ML.
5. **Current pandas.** Newer pandas (copy-on-write, the default in pandas 3) does not change `df` through chained
   assignment such as `df[df.a > 0]["b"] = 1`. The book teaches only `df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1`, which is correct in
   every version. Do not copy code from older books without checking it.

## The book's content {#sec-content}

One part for each topic. Each part has one to three notebooks (pages), so a student can read one page in about
15 to 25 minutes. The "Lecture" column is the course's order. It is only here, never in the book (D4). The pages
(`jb/chapters/`, in `jb/_toc.yml`): 00 Colab, Thonny and other IDEs; 01 A first machine-learning example; 02 What
does a model learn?; 03 From lists to NumPy arrays; 04 Indexing, slicing and arithmetic; 05 Comparisons and Boolean
masks; 06 Two-dimensional arrays; 07 Series and DataFrames; 08 Reading and describing data; 09 Selecting with loc
and iloc; 10 Filtering rows; 11 New columns and sorting; 12 Grouping and summarizing; 13 Preparing data for machine
learning; 14 Guided project: delivery times; 15 Independent project: advertising and sales; 16 Common errors and how
to fix them; 17 Cheat sheet; 18 The datasets; 19 Further reading. The two projects share the part "Putting it
together".

| Part | Lecture | Pages | What students can do after it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Using this book | before the first | **Colab, Thonny and other IDEs**: open a chapter in Colab (the launch button and the badge), run cells, save a copy to Drive; **the same code in Thonny**: install numpy, pandas, scikit-learn and matplotlib with Tools > Manage packages, **see the installed versions and upgrade a package** (D7), **wrap the last expression in `print()`**, or type it in the Shell; charts need `plt.show()` and Thonny waits until the chart window closes; reading data from a URL or from a downloaded file (the script's folder); a short note on VS Code, Spyder and local Jupyter; what to do when something fails | Run a chapter's code in Colab and in Thonny |
| Why NumPy and pandas? | 1 | **A first machine-learning example** (a demonstration): a business question; CSV → DataFrame → predictors `X` and target `y` → train/test split → three models → predictions → compare the error (MAE). **What a model optimizes** (the objective function in plain words: the model picks numbers that make the average squared error small). **The point:** most lines of the code are pandas and NumPy. That is what the next parts teach | Explain the ML workflow in words; run the provided code |
| NumPy arrays | 2 | **Lists versus arrays** (arithmetic on a whole column at once; speed in one sentence); `np.array()`; `dtype`; indexing and slicing; **vectorized arithmetic**; a few functions (`np.round`, `np.sqrt`) | Create arrays and compute with them without loops |
| Working with arrays | 3 | **Comparisons and Boolean masks**; filtering with a mask; `sum`, `mean`, `min`, `max`, counting with `mask.sum()`. **2-D arrays**: rows, columns, `shape`, `axis=0` and `axis=1`. **Bridge to ML**: `X` is 2-D, `y` is 1-D; `X.shape`, `y.shape`; `df.to_numpy()` (a preview) | Filter and summarize arrays; read `shape` |
| pandas: first steps | 4 | **Series and DataFrame**; `pd.read_csv()`; `head()`, `tail()`, `shape`, `columns`, `dtypes`, `info()`, `describe()`; selecting one column and several columns | Load a CSV and describe it |
| pandas: selecting and changing data | 5 | **`loc` and `iloc`**; Boolean filtering with `&`, `|`, `~` and parentheses; `isin()`; **new columns from old ones**; `sort_values()`; the rule `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` | Answer "which rows?" questions; add calculated columns |
| pandas: summarizing and preparing data | 6 | **`value_counts()`, `groupby()` with `mean`/`sum`/`count`, `agg()`**; one simple chart (`df.plot(...)`). **Preparing data for ML**: `isna().sum()`, `dropna()`, `fillna()`, `pd.get_dummies()`, choosing `X` and `y` | Summarize by group; make a dataset ready for scikit-learn |
| Putting it together I | 7 | **A guided project** on a new business dataset: read, inspect, clean, choose `X` and `y`, run the prepared model code, compare the models, say what the result means for the business | Do the full workflow with guidance |
| Putting it together II | 8 | **An independent project** on another dataset, with a checklist and a short written interpretation | Do the full workflow alone |
| Appendices | — | **Common errors** (`FileNotFoundError`, `KeyError`, `ModuleNotFoundError`, shape mismatch, `NaN` in `fit`, a chained-assignment warning) with the fix for each; **a one-page cheat sheet**; **the datasets** (a data dictionary for each CSV); **further reading** | — |

**Further reading** (links per chapter, never the main text): "NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners"
(numpy.org) for the NumPy parts; the pandas "Getting started" tutorials (pandas.pydata.org) for the pandas parts;
Downey, *Elements of Data Science*, chapters 3 and 7 (Green Tea Press); McKinney, *Python for Data Analysis* 3rd
ed., as a reference (some of its pandas code predates current pandas).

No new ML algorithm or evaluation method after the first part. The two projects practice the Python skills and
the workflow; they do not teach model building.

### The datasets {#sec-datasets}

`data/make_data.py` (with `--help`) writes every CSV with a fixed seed; the CSVs are committed too. The page
`jb/chapters/18-datasets.md` describes every column. The files:

| File | Rows | Used in | Content |
|---|---|---|---|
| `customers.csv` | 500 | the first ML example; preparing data | age, region (text), months as customer, visits per month, average basket, a few `NaN`; target: annual spend |
| `sales.csv` | 2,000 | the pandas parts | date, store, region, product category, units, unit price, discount; good for `groupby` |
| `deliveries.csv` | 500 | the guided project | food deliveries: distance, items, time of day, weather, driver experience; target: minutes; `NaN` in a number and a text column |
| `marketing.csv` | 520 | the independent project | weekly sales by region with TV and online advertising, price, promotion; target: units sold; `NaN` in a number and a text column |

Keep printed tables to six columns or fewer, so they do not wrap in Thonny's Shell.

## Writing rules for the notebooks {#sec-writing}

The rules are in one place: the `notebook-conventions` skill (`.claude/skills/notebook-conventions/SKILL.md`). In
short: business students who know basic Python; the tone of *Think Python*; one idea per section; no timing (D4);
Colab-first code that also runs in Thonny with only `print()` added; data only from `DATA_URL`; no stored outputs;
practice questions (Easy, Medium, Hard, Challenge) with collapsed answers; code that works in pandas 2 and 3.

Two decisions of 2026-11-23, tested in a build (the skill has the formats):

- **Answers are HTML `<details class="yr-answer">` blocks, not MyST dropdowns.** Colab shows a MyST directive
  (`:::{admonition}`) as raw text, so students would see every answer at once. `<details>` stays closed on the
  website and in Colab.
- **Boxes ("Try it", "Common mistake", "In Thonny", "Note") are markdown block quotes.** MyST admonitions show as raw
  text in Colab, and HTML admonitions do not format markdown in Colab.

## Step 3: the book's infrastructure {#sec-step3}

Done 2026-11-23. The checkers are `tools/check_notebooks.py` (lint, portability, answers format, no timing, table
of contents, `--help`), `tools/run_as_script.py` (the Thonny check and the answers check; run with `.venv` and
with `.venv-newest`), `data/make_data.py --check` (data) and the build itself (execution, `-W`). The workflow runs
them all before it publishes, and runs the Thonny check with the newest versions in a separate job. Two more
tools: `tools/localdata/sitecustomize.py` makes the data URLs read `data/` during checks and builds, and
`tools/nbtext.py` converts a chapter between a notebook and a plain-text draft. The skills: `notebook-conventions`,
`check-notebooks`, `build-book`, `add-page`, `deploy-book` (none copied from yrThinkPython; written for this book).
The original list:

1. **Layout:**

   | Path | What it holds |
   |---|---|
   | `jb/_config.yml`, `jb/_toc.yml`, `jb/intro.md` | The Jupyter Book |
   | `jb/chapters/*.ipynb` | The chapters (no stored outputs) |
   | `jb/subjexts-labels.md` | The "Table of contents by label" page (from yrProject's subjexts part; never edit or rename it) |
   | `data/` | `make_data.py` and the CSVs |
   | `requirements.txt` | Colab's versions (D7), `jupyter-book<2` and the build packages |
   | `.github/workflows/deploy-book.yml` | Build and publish on a push to `main` (D6) |
   | `.claude/skills/*/` | The skills, with their checkers next to them |

2. **`jb/_toc.yml`:** the first part is `- caption: Table of contents by label` with `chapters: - file:
   subjexts-labels`. Then one part for each topic, with topic names only (D4). The build uses
   `execute_notebooks: force`; change that only if it causes a problem.
3. **Python for building:** `.venv` (D12), from `requirements.txt`.
4. **The workflow** `.github/workflows/deploy-book.yml` (done 2026-11-23, without the checks): on a push to `main`
   and by hand, install `requirements.txt`, `jb build jb`, push `jb/_build/html` to `gh-pages`. Add the checks
   (item 5) as its first steps.
5. **Checkers** (each with `--help`; each prints `OK` or the problems; the workflow runs them first):
   - **Notebook lint:** valid JSON, cell ids, no stored outputs, the first cell has the title and the correct
     Colab badge for its own path, every notebook is in `_toc.yml`, scripts have `--help`.
   - **Portability:** no `%`/`!` lines, no `google.colab`, no `display(`, no local or Drive data paths.
   - **Execution:** run every notebook top to bottom with the pinned versions, and again with the newest releases
     (D7).
   - **Thonny check:** convert each notebook to a script (wrap a bare last expression of each cell in `print()`),
     and run it with plain `python`, as Thonny does. This proves the "only `print()` changes" rule.
   - **Answers:** run the code in every practice answer.
   - **Data:** `data/make_data.py --check` regenerates the CSVs in a temporary folder and compares them with the
     committed ones.
6. **Skills:** build, check, notebook conventions, add a page, deploy, practice questions. Adapt yrThinkPython's
   (`build-book`, `check-notebooks`, `notebook-conventions`, `add-page`, `deploy-book`, `yr-review-questions`)
   where they fit, without its Think Python parts (Allen Downey, upstream syncing, `%%expect`, solution overlays,
   `yr/` pages, the Colab-like kernel). List each copy in @sec-copies. Add a fill-in-the-blank skill only if the
   instructor wants such notebooks.
7. **`AGENTS.md` project rules** (outside the yrProject blocks): the writing rules (@sec-writing); the checkers to
   run before a commit; topic branches, and push to `main` only when the instructor asks; never rename a published
   notebook; the versions (D7); "labels live on subjexts, not in this repository".
8. **Build once** locally and check: no warnings, all checkers `OK`.

## Step 4: plug the book into subjexts (yrS4) {#sec-step4}

Do this early (right after Step 3), so the instructor can review chapters with author notes. Items 1 and 2 change
files in the yrS4 repository: **do them only with the instructor's OK**, or let the instructor run them.

1. From the yrS4 repository (check `git status` first: other sessions work there):

   ```bash
   scripts/plug-in-book.sh --manifest-only --jupyter-book /home/yitz/Dropbox/_yrQuarto-master/yr-pre-ml pre-ml \
     "What is Machine Learning? Prerequisite material for getting started" https://y-rosenthal.github.io/yr-pre-ml/
   ```

2. Check `packages/pre-ml.yml` against `packages/thinkpython.yml`: `generator: jupyter-book`;
   `license: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0`; `source.repo: y-rosenthal/yr-pre-ml`; `source.local`; `source.toc: jb/_toc.yml`;
   `overlay.hide_from_tutor: ["details.yr-answer"]` (the answers, @sec-writing); no `page_version_suffix`; `ai.tutor: true`. Commit that
   one file in yrS4 by path.
3. **(instructor runs)** `node cli/bin/yrS4.mjs packages push pre-ml`.
4. **Sections.** The course sections must list the package, or students see only the instructor's own labels.
   Ask the instructor which sections. Adding the package to them is a change in yrS4 (`yrS4 seed`): do it in a
   chat in the yrS4 repository; the live write is **(instructor runs)**.
5. After each publish: **(instructor runs)** `node cli/bin/yrS4.mjs scan y-rosenthal/pre-ml`. The scan learns the
   pages and reports orphaned marks.
6. Labels such as "Covered in Lecture 3" are made in the subjexts panel or with `yrS4 teach`, not in this
   repository.

## Step 5: write the content {#sec-step5}

Done 2026-11-23 for all the pages (the instructor asked to finish and publish the whole book). Chapters 00 to 02
were written first, as models; helper agents wrote the others from one brief (the outline above and the
`notebook-conventions` skill), and two independent reviews of the executed pages led to fixes (wrong claims, for
example that every scikit-learn model refuses missing values; references; Colab's exact messages). Items 3 and 4 below,
the instructor's review in the local build or on the website and the test in Colab and in Thonny on Windows and
Mac, are still to do; the instructor's changes can come as subjexts note packets.

Order: the "Colab, Thonny and other IDEs" chapter and "Why NumPy and pandas?" first (with `customers.csv`), then
one part at a time. For each part:

1. Write the notebooks (@sec-writing) and their practice questions.
2. Run the checkers and build locally.
3. Ask the instructor to read it in the local build. The instructor can mark it up with subjexts author notes and
   in-place edits, export a note packet, and give it to the chat; apply it with the `subjexts` skill
   (`apply-notes` procedure in yrS4).
4. The instructor runs the part's code in Colab and in Thonny (at least one Windows and one Mac machine) before
   the class uses it.

## Phases {#sec-phases}

| Phase | Work | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| A | Steps 0, 2, 3 and Step 4 items 1–3; `make_data.py`; the IDE chapter; "Why NumPy and pandas?" | The instructor ran the first part in Colab and Thonny; the build passes; subjexts works on the local build |
| B | The NumPy and pandas parts, one at a time, each reviewed before the next | Checkers `OK`; the instructor's notes applied |
